implementation_notes: Swift's value semantics do most of the work: Array is a struct with copy-on-write storage, so any array a caller receives is already isolated - mutating the received copy cannot touch the owner's array (the standard-library documentation: 'Multiple copies of an array share the same storage until you modify one of the copies'). The idiomatic declaration is therefore `private(set) var courses: [Course] = []`, which the Swift book describes as giving the setter a lower access level than the getter so the type can change the value internally while presenting a read-only property to the outside. Membership changes go through addCourse/removeCourse; a computed property returning a copy is only needed when the stored representation differs from the published one.
pitfalls: Value semantics protect membership, not elements: an array of class instances shares the objects, so `person.courses[0].name = ...` still mutates what the owner sees.

`private(set)` restricts assignment only; if the property's type is a class-based collection (an NSArray-backed wrapper or a custom reference type), handing it out hands out shared mutable state - prefer Array/Dictionary/Set.

Mutating methods must be `mutating` on structs and cannot be called on a `let` instance; if the owner needs identity or shared mutation, model it as a class and guard the collection explicitly with a computed property.
A getter that returns the stored array is cheap (COW), but a getter that returns an NSMutableArray or a custom reference collection reintroduces aliasing.
